media_work.title: Anatomy of Injustice: A Murder Case Gone Wrong
media_work.focus_or_theme: Detailed examination of a single wrongful conviction case, racial bias in the justice system, death penalty issues
media_work.key_statistics: The book that helped free an innocent man who had spent twenty-seven years on death row

key_quotes_raw: "Masterful... Eloquent, important, and accessible... The book of the century about the death penalty." —Andrew Cohen, The Atlantic

"A genuine whodunit, a page-turner, and a tale of redemption. And it's all true. For all that, however, Anatomy of Injustice is also a blistering indictment of the death penalty." —Laura Miller, Salon.com
"Gripping and enraging... Bonner's book is not a treatise against the death penalty. Rather, it is a look at what happens in America's justice system when justice is absent." —The Economist
systemic_issues_raw: Racial discrimination in the criminal justice system
Inadequate defense representation for poor defendants
Flaws in the appeals process for death penalty cases
Difficulties in proving innocence after conviction
Systemic resistance to acknowledging and correcting wrongful convictions
policy_recommendations_raw: Improved standards for defense counsel in capital cases
Enhanced procedures for handling and preserving evidence
Greater scrutiny of cases involving racial disparities
Reforms to make it easier to challenge wrongful convictions
additional_resources_raw: After his release, Edward Lee Elmore filed a federal lawsuit against Greenwood County for his wrongful conviction
The case has been cited in discussions about compensation for the wrongfully convicted in South Carolina

research_notes_other.this_book_is_particularly_valuable_for_o:
1. Provides an in-depth examination of a single case that exemplifies multiple systemic issues in the criminal justice system
2. Highlights the intersection of race, mental disability, and economic disadvantage in wrongful convictions
3. Documents the extraordinary length of time (nearly 30 years) that an innocent person spent incarcerated
4. Demonstrates the difficulty of overturning wrongful convictions even with substantial evidence of innocence
5. Shows how a book can contribute to public awareness and ultimately help secure an exoneration
6. Examines the death penalty system through the lens of a specific case
The book received significant critical acclaim and was described by reviewers as one of the most important books on the death penalty and wrongful convictions. Written by Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist Raymond Bonner, it combines investigative reporting with legal analysis to create what reviewers called a "seductive" and "compelling" narrative that educates readers about systemic injustices while telling a powerful human story.

media_item.item_title: Book Content: Anatomy of Injustice: A Murder Case Gone Wrong
media_item.focus_or_theme: Detailed examination of a single wrongful conviction case, racial bias in the justice system, death penalty issues
media_item.summary_notes: An in-depth examination of Edward Lee Elmore's wrongful conviction for murder, highlighting systemic issues like racial bias, prosecutorial misconduct, inadequate defense, and flaws in the death penalty appeals process.  The book details Elmore's nearly 30 years on death row and his eventual release in 2012. It's presented as a compelling narrative that educates readers about systemic injustices while telling a powerful human story and received significant critical acclaim.
media_item.case_details_raw: Edward Lee Elmore was wrongfully convicted in 1982 for the murder of Dorothy Edwards in Greenwood, South Carolina.  He spent nearly 30 years incarcerated, much of it on death row, before his release in 2012 after reaching an agreement with the state. His case exemplified multiple systemic issues within the criminal justice system.

featured_individuals.crime_convicted_of: Murder of Dorothy Edwards, an elderly white widow
contributing_factors_raw: Racial bias (Black man accused of killing white woman in the South)
Mental disability (Elmore was described as "semi-literate" and "mentally retarded")
featured_individuals.status_raw: Released in 2012 after reaching an agreement with the state of South Carolina
featured_individuals.cross_reference: Similar themes to "Just Mercy" by Bryan Stevenson and "The Innocent Man" by John Grisham
